summary: A 1978 Telnet option for SUPDUP-Output, used together with the SUPDUP protocol to carry its display output over Telnet. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The SUPDUP-OUTPUT option lets a server send display-control instructions through a Telnet connection. The user side describes its terminal first, so the server can send suitable screen commands.

questions: what is the telnet supdup-output option
how does supdup output work over telnet
subtitle: A Telnet option for carrying SUPDUP screen-control output while Telnet remains active.

tldr.problem: Display programs on a server needed screen control without changing the whole Telnet connection to the SUPDUP protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The user sends terminal parameters after negotiation, and the server sends SUPDUP display codes in subnegotiation blocks.
tldr.outcome: Telnet commands remain valid, and without display blocks the connection behaves like normal Telnet.

today: RFC 749 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Screen Control Without Replacing Telnet
sections.content:
SUPDUP-OUTPUT provides access to the virtual display support of SUPDUP within a standard Telnet connection. Unlike the full SUPDUP protocol, it does not hand all communication and screen management to the server for the duration of the connection.

A display-oriented server program can control the user's screen explicitly, while Telnet stays active. Telnet commands such as IAC IP remain valid.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can control parts of the display without taking over the whole connection. Regular Telnet commands still work.

sections.title: Negotiation and Terminal Parameters
sections.content:
Only the server Telnet process may initiate this option, using IAC WILL SUPDUP-OUTPUT. The user Telnet process accepts with IAC DO SUPDUP-OUTPUT or refuses with IAC DON'T SUPDUP-OUTPUT. After accepting, it immediately sends terminal parameters in a subnegotiation with command code 1.

The terminal parameters describe the user's terminal as specified by RFC 734. Once the server receives them, it may send SUPDUP-OUTPUT blocks.
sections.plainLanguage: The server offers the option. If the user accepts, the user side sends terminal details before the server sends screen-control data.

sections.title: Screen-Control Blocks and Defaults
sections.content:
A server sends command code 2, a count N, the SUPDUP output codes and printing characters, then two bytes for the expected cursor coordinates. The count may be zero and cannot exceed 254. A multi-byte TDCODE sequence must not be split across blocks, and the output-reset code must not be sent.

The default is WON'T and DON'T, so no SUPDUP-OUTPUT messages may be transmitted unless the option is negotiated. The option does not define input; NVT input is the default.
sections.plainLanguage: The server sends a counted list of screen actions and the expected cursor position. Without agreement, no screen-control messages are sent.
